newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan Prime View tackles Japan's monitor monopoly.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan Prime View tackles Japan's monitor monopoly.

text.p: For years, Japan's technology giants have monopolised the global mini-monitor market in the same way their Taiwanese counterparts have dominated production of the bigger displays.
Now, Taiwan's Prime View International says it is ready to step out of its traditional niche and challenge the likes of Toshiba and Hitachi at their own game.
"We believe our products will be competitive against the Japanese makes because our products have better resolution at the same price levels," company president Lee Sheh-nan told Reuters.

Prime View, which for the past four years has focused exclusively on research and development, said it would become the first Taiwan firm to produce 1.8- and 2.5-inch miniature monitors by the first quarter of 1997.
The company, which also would make five-inch monitors in 1997, has forecast sales revenue at T$2.5 billion (US$90.9 million) for its inaugural production year.
Prime View, capitalised at T$1.5 billion and 88 percent owned by paper manufacturer Yuen Foong Yu, expected an initial production capacity of 90,000 monitors per month.
The company plans to quadruple this capacity and extend production to include the most popular monitor -- the 12.1-inch display -- by the end of 1998.
"We are beginning with the smaller models because chip size determines production yield, and therefore production yield can easily be achieved (with the smaller displays)," Lee said.
"After our production runs up to a satisfactory level, we will get into the larger-size panels," he added.
A foray into the market would lock Prime View in competition with leading monitor makers Acer Peripherals, Philips Taiwan and Liteon Technology
Most of Taiwan's monitor makers opt to produce larger models because of high demand from desktop and notebook computers.
Prime View estimates global demand for the 12.1-inch displays, used mainly for computer monitors, to reach a hefty 8.2 million sets in 1996 and more than 30 million in 1999.

By comparison, demand for the five-inch-and-under displays, used in various media from video camcorders to airplane applications, stood at nine million sets in 1996 and is seen rising to 16.9 million in 1999.
For large and small displays, the monitor market will follow where computer technology takes it.

"New application for the small displays is just beginning," said Lee. "Before, the technology was too expensive. Now, it's becoming very common and everybody has ideas on where to use the technology."
While Prime View sets its immediate sights on computer-rich customers in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, it has visions of tapping into a currently dormant but potentially explosive market -- China.
"But for that kind of population, price is a big issue," he added, noting that most of communist China's 1.2 billion people have buying power far below that of Taiwan's 21 million.
But Lee predicted that China's annual demand for monitors would top 10 million units in a few years.
"The key factors are whether the prices for the monitors are reduced and the living standard in China rises," Lee said. ($US=T$27.5)
